text: Recognition → Early CPR → Early defibrillation → Early ACLS → Post-cardiac arrest care. Each link critical: within 10 min CPR crucial, defibrillation within 3-5 min ideal, ACLS medications timely, post-arrest TTM/interventions. Survival decreases ~10%/min without defibrillation in VF. Public access defibrillation (PAD) programs improve outcomes. Community CPR training essential.

metadata.topic: Chain of survival for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest

text: No-flow time = time from arrest to start of CPR. Low-flow time = duration of CPR. Outcomes inversely correlated with both. Neurologic recovery unlikely if no-flow >10 min (exceptions: profound hypothermia, submersion). Low-flow >30 min with poor prognostic indicators → consider stopping resuscitation. Young patients/reversible cause may warrant longer resuscitation. Bystander CPR crucial for reducing no-flow time.

metadata.topic: Cardiac arrest no-flow and low-flow time

text: Biphasic defibrillation (most modern AEDs) safer and equally effective as monophasic. Energy: 120-200 J for biphasic, 360 J for monophasic (not used). Defibrillation works by: depolarizing entire heart → interrupting reentrant circuit. VF recurs within seconds if no intervention (CPR must follow immediately). Higher energy not better beyond effective dose. Manual defibrillator preferred (allows synchronization for VT). AED automated detection of shockable rhythm.

Rate: 100-120 compressions/min. Depth: 2-2.4 inches (5-6 cm) in adults. Recoil: allow full chest recoil between compressions (not removing hand). Ventilation: balance compressions with rescue breaths in witnessed arrest (30:2), compression-only in asystole/PEA. Avoid excessive ventilation (causes gastric inflation, hyperinflation impairs venous return). Minimize interruptions to compressions (<10 sec). Mechanical CPR devices allow sustained high-quality compressions.

Pediatric: depth 2 inches (1/3 chest depth), rate 100-120, compression-only acceptable. Pregnant: leftward uterine displacement, consider perimortem cesarean. Elderly: assess for DNR, may have fragile ribs. Obese: adequate depth may require increased effort. Trauma: cervical spine precautions initially, then standard ACLS. Drowning: air exchange critical (may need rescue breathing first). Hypothermia: slow assessment, prolong resuscitation attempts.

Portable device analyzes ECG → determines if shock indicated. Visible electrode pads adhere to chest (bare skin). Operator follows voice prompts (continue CPR, stand clear, etc). Highly sensitive/specific for VF/PVT. Should be deployed immediately in any unresponsive adult with no pulse. PAD programs in public spaces (airports, sports venues) improve access to defibrillation. Training simple—designed for layperson use.

IV (intravenous) preferred—reliable access, rapid delivery. IO (intraosseous) if no IV access available (proximal humerus or tibia). Both equally effective. ETT (endotracheal tube) accessible but absorption unpredictable (avoid if IV/IO feasible). IM epinephrine useful in specific scenarios (anaphylaxis, remote settings). All ACLS medications can be given IV/IO; only some via ETT (epinephrine, lidocaine, atropine, vasopressin—remember LEAN).

Usually due to severe bronchospasm/hypoxemia. Treat: aggressive CPR, consider magnesium (2 g IV), terbutaline (10 mcg IV, repeat), epinephrine standard dose. Minimize triggering factors (avoid morphine/atracurium if possible). Prolonged CPR may be needed (brain more resistant to hypoxemia with hypercarbia). Difficult intubation anticipated. Post-ROSC: aggressive bronchodilators, may need ECMO if conventional CPR fails.

Hypoxemia + reduced O2 carrying capacity = rapid deterioration. RBCs crucial for oxygen transport. Standard ACLS applies but outcome poor without transfusion. Type O negative blood immediately if available. Goal: maintain Hb >7-10 g/dL post-ROSC (higher targets may increase thrombotic risk). Massive transfusion protocol if ongoing hemorrhage. Prolonged CPR may be needed (brain paradoxically tolerates hypoxemia better in acute anemia).

Sepsis can cause cardiac arrest (septic cardiomyopathy, distributive shock). CPR combined with immediate antibiotics, source control, vasopressors. Sepsis-related VF less responsive to standard ACLS. Consider extended resuscitation effort (usually improved prognosis if source reversible). Post-ROSC: continue antibiotics, ICU-level care, source control (drainage of abscess, etc). Lactate elevation common (not necessarily prognostic if resolves).

Asystole alone not indication to stop if reversible cause possible. Consider: patient age, comorbidities, witnessed arrest, no-flow time, response to resuscitation (any improvement?), reversible cause identified? Hypothermia is exception (continue until rewarmed). ETCO2 <10 throughout resuscitation → poor prognosis. Severe head injury/trauma → assess neurologic status post-ROSC. Family preferences if known (DNR order). Ethical discussions important.

Epinephrine: 1 mg IV every 3-5 min. Amiodarone: 300 mg first dose, 150 mg second dose, then 150 mg as often as every 5-10 min (max 2.2 g/day). Atropine (if used): 0.5-1 mg every 3-5 min (max 3 mg total). Sodium bicarbonate: 1 mEq/kg initially, repeat every 5-10 min. Calcium: 5-10 mL of 10% solution IV push. Spacing prevents drug interactions/cumulative toxicity. IV flushes between medications recommended. Document timing carefully.

Contemporary practice: allowing family at bedside during resuscitation. May improve grief processing, family understanding of death. No negative impact on team performance if organized. Designated staff member to support family. Debrief with family post-code (explain what happened, prognosis). Support services (chaplaincy, social work) helpful. Document family presence in medical record. Increases transparency/trust.

Chest X-ray: assess for aspiration, pneumothorax, rib fractures (CPR complications). ECG: identify underlying rhythm (STEMI, Brugada, Long QT). Head CT: consider if altered mental status, concern for intracranial process. Troponin/CK-MB: assess for MI (elevated post-arrest anyway from CPR). Lactate: marker of tissue hypoperfusion (trends useful). Blood gas: respiratory status, metabolic acidosis degree. Consider angiography if STEMI presentation.

ECMO/ECPR (extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation) for profound hypothermia (<20°C) in cardiac arrest. Provides rapid rewarming while supporting circulation. Transfers heat to blood externally. May achieve full recovery even after prolonged arrest in profound hypothermia (>1 hour CPR reported with good outcome). Requires: ECMO-capable center, rapid transport, experienced team. Exceptional survival rates possible. Travel to ECMO center justified.

Three or more ectopic foci in atria → irregular tachycardia. ECG: variable P-wave morphology, variable PR intervals, irregular rate (100-150 typically). Associated with: COPD (most common), hypoxemia, pulmonary HTN, hyperthyroidism, hypokalemia, digoxin toxicity. Treatment: beta-blockers (rate control), calcium channel blockers, treat underlying cause (oxygenation, correct K+). Avoid adenosine (ineffective for MAT, may cause AVN block). Digoxin not first-line. Prognosis depends on underlying disease.

Rapid regular atrial rhythm with visible P waves at rate 100-250 bpm. Single focus in atrium (unlike MAT). Types: sinus tachycardia (normal P waves, appropriate HR for clinical status), ectopic atrial tachycardia (abnormal P morphology, inappropriate HR). Treatment: beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, class IC antiarrhythmics (flecainide, propafenone), amiodarone. Ablation if refractory. Usually benign prognosis if structural heart disease excluded.

metadata.topic: Atrial tachycardia and ectopic atrial tachycardia

text: Rhythm originates in AV junction (around AV node). Rate 100-150 bpm, narrow QRS, P waves buried in QRS (RP <100 ms) or immediately after. Retrograde conduction to atria (may see retrograde P after QRS). Regular rhythm. Causes: digoxin toxicity (most common cause of junctional tachycardia), enhanced AV nodal automaticity, after cardiac surgery. Treatment: digoxin toxicity requires discontinuation, potassium correction, magnesium, antidigoxin Fab if needed. Beta-blockers, CCB also helpful.

ECG: type 1 pattern = coved ST elevation V1-V2 with negative T wave (mimics RBBB with ST elevation). Diagnostic = <1 mV ST elevation. Type II/III patterns less specific. Brugada syndrome = type 1 pattern + symptoms (syncope, nocturnal agonal respirations, cardiac arrest). Risk factors: fever, drugs (flecainide, propafenone), hyperthermia. Mechanism: sodium channel mutation. Cellular uncoupling of early phases of ventricular repolarization. ICD recommended for symptomatic patients.

Early repolarization = J point elevation (junction between QRS and ST segment) in V2-V3. Often normal finding, especially in young males, athletes. Osborn wave (prominent J wave) seen in hypothermia. Early repolarization can predispose to VF in some individuals. Risk increased if: extensive J wave elevation (>2 mm), ST-segment horizontal/descending, diffuse pattern, high-risk genotype (DCHS1 mutation). Usually asymptomatic. Management: ICD if symptomatic, watchful waiting if asymptomatic.

MI frequently triggers arrhythmias. Anterior MI (STEMI): VT, VF (especially first 48h). Inferior MI: bradycardia, AV block (from RV involvement), ventricular ectopy. Reciprocal inferior changes with anterior STEMI may show atrial arrhythmias. Reperfusion arrhythmias: accelerated idioventricular rhythm (AIVR) indicates successful reperfusion (benign). Treatment: revascularization (PCI/CABG) critical. Beta-blockers reduce arrhythmia risk post-MI. Antiarrhythmics secondary. ICD if EF drops post-MI.

Therapeutic window narrow (0.8-2 ng/mL). Toxicity presents with: nausea/vomiting (earliest sign), arrhythmias. Arrhythmias from digoxin: PACs, PVCs, atrial tachycardia with AV block, junctional tachycardia, VT, complete heart block (severe). Combination arrhythmias possible (e.g., atrial tach + AV block = highly specific for digoxin toxicity). Risk factors: hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, renal failure, drug interactions (amiodarone, verapamil increase digoxin levels). Treatment: stop digoxin, correct K+/Mg2+, antidigoxin Fab for severe toxicity.

Multiple organ systems affected. Thyroid: hyper/hypothyroidism (most common, 1-5% of patients). Lung: pulmonary fibrosis (rare, 1%, but serious). Liver: hepatotoxicity (monitor LFTs). Cornea: microdeposits (vision usually preserved). Skin: blue-gray discoloration. Neurologic: tremor, neuropathy. Cardiac: torsades de pointes (QT prolongation), bradycardia, AV block, negative inotropic effect (can worsen HF initially). Monitoring: baseline TSH, FT4, LFTs, ECG. Consider discontinuation if toxicity. Half-life very long (weeks-months).

QT interval reflects ventricular repolarization duration. Corrected QT (QTc) adjusts for heart rate. Normal QTc <440 ms males, <460 ms females. Prolongation risk factors: antiarrhythmic drugs (sotalol, dofetilide, amiodarone), antibiotics (fluoroquinolones, macrolides), antipsychotics (haloperidol, clozapine), antiretrovirals, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia, female sex, bradycardia. Torsades de pointes risk increases substantially if QTc >500 ms. Management: avoid QT-prolonging drugs, correct electrolytes, beta-blockers if Long QT syndrome.

Pro-arrhythmic effects from: increased automaticity (sympathomimetics, hyperthyroidism), triggered activity (digoxin toxicity, early afterdepolarizations from QT prolongation, delayed afterdepolarizations), reentry (flecainide paradoxically slowing conduction to facilitate reentry). Class IC antiarrhythmics (flecainide, propafenone) particularly pro-arrhythmic in structural heart disease (avoid post-MI). Some drugs: sotalol (QT prolongation), verapamil (AV block risk). Risk-benefit assessment critical before antiarrhythmic use.

Indications: AVNRT (90% success), AVRT (95% success), typical atrial flutter (>95% success), atrial fibrillation (70-80% for paroxysmal, 50-60% for persistent), VT (50-80% depending on mechanism). Procedure: catheter-based endovascular approach, identify arrhythmia site, ablate tissue (heat causes scar formation blocking conduction). Risks: vascular injury, stroke (AF ablation), perforation, thromboembolism. Anesthesia: sedation or general. Success depends on: mechanism identification, accessible site, expertise of operator. Cure possible (no lifelong antiarrhythmics).

metadata.topic: Radiofrequency ablation indications and success rates

text: Alternative to radiofrequency: uses extreme cold (cryogenic energy) to freeze tissue. Potential advantages: ability to test effect before committing (freeze lesion reversible initially), better contact in challenging anatomy, reduced perforation risk (adhesive effect of ice). Used for: AVNRT (similar success to RF), some accessory pathways, AF (emerging). Success rates: comparable to RF ablation. Cost higher than RF. Less operator experience compared to RF (more recently introduced). Integration with imaging improving outcomes.

Electronic device implanted in chest with lead(s) to heart. Monitors rhythm → detects VT/VF → delivers shock (defibrillation) automatically. Indications: prior cardiac arrest from VT/VF (secondary prevention), EF <35% with ischemic cardiomyopathy (primary prevention), genetic syndromes (Long QT, Brugada, CPVT). ICD improved survival ~20-30% in appropriate populations (MADIT trials). Risks: inappropriate shocks (usually for SVT), lead failure, infection. Patients can hear/feel shock (painful, frightening). Psychological support important.

Symptomatic bradycardia (SSS, AV block) refractory to medical therapy. Sinus node disease with HR <40 or pauses >3 sec. High-degree AV block (Mobitz II, complete heart block). Bifascicular block + syncope (concerning for progressing to CHB). Pacer modes: VVI (ventricular demand, no atrial sensing), AAI (atrial, sinus node disease), DDD (dual-chamber, most physiologic). Rate-adaptive pacing (increases rate with activity). Risk: infection, lead fracture, oversensing/undersensing. Longevity: 10-15 years typical.

Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy: paces both ventricles simultaneously to improve synchrony (RV and LV contracting together vs. out of sync in LBBB). Indications: HFrEF (EF <35%), QRS >120 ms (especially LBBB pattern), NYHA Class III-IV on optimal medical therapy. CRT improves EF, symptoms, exercise tolerance, mortality (25-30% reduction). Response rate ~60-70% (super-responders vs. non-responders). Can combine with ICD (CRT-D) for rhythm and resynchronization therapy. Requires optimization (AV delay, VV delay) post-implant.

Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) / pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) bind Toll-like receptors (TLRs) on immune cells. Triggers innate immune cascade: NF-kB activation, massive pro-inflammatory cytokine release (TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-6). Cytokines cause: endothelial dysfunction (increased permeability, edema), vasodilation (decreased SVR), myocardial depression (TNF-alpha cardiotoxic), microvascular dysfunction (shunting, capillary closure), mitochondrial dysfunction (impaired aerobic metabolism). Result: distributive shock with tissue hypoperfusion despite high CO initially. Late shock: multi-organ failure.

Rapid source control critical: remove infected device (central line, urinary catheter), drain abscess, necrotizing fasciitis requires immediate debridement, perforated viscus requires surgery. Source control should NOT be delayed for diagnostics (imaging while starting antibiotics/vasopressors). Timing matter: source control within 12h optimal (mortality increases with delay beyond 12-24h). Surgery vs. percutaneous drainage decision based on feasibility/patient status. Repeat procedures may be needed.

Bundle approach: 1-hour bundle (lactate measurement, blood cultures, broad-spectrum antibiotics, fluid bolus 30 mL/kg if hypotensive, vasopressor if MAP <65 after fluids). 6-hour bundle (reassess perfusion, repeat lactate, repeat fluid assessment, adjust therapy). De-escalation: narrow antibiotics once culture results available (48-72h). Duration: typically 7-10 days total (re-evaluate daily). Goals: ScvO2 >70%, MAP >65, urine output >0.5 mL/kg/h, lactate normalization. Early recognition and treatment improve outcomes.

RV dysfunction common in sepsis (septic cardiomyopathy). Mechanisms: myocardial depression from TNF, elevated afterload (pulmonary HTN from ARDS, excessive vasopressors), hypovolemia. Presents with: elevated CVP despite low PAWP, reduced RV output, tricuspid regurgitation. Echo shows RV dilation, reduced function, septal flattening. Treatment: optimize preload (careful fluid management), reduce afterload (inhaled nitric oxide, milrinone), inotropes (dobutamine, milrinone), pulmonary vasodilators. Poor prognosis if RV failure severe.

metadata.topic: Right ventricular failure in septic shock

text: Early aggressive fluids improve survival (RIVERS trial, EGDT). Goal: MAP >65 (usually requires 30 mL/kg initial bolus). Balanced crystalloids (lactated Ringer, Plasmalyte) preferred over normal saline (hyperchloremic acidosis risk). Albumin NOT superior to crystalloids in general sepsis (SAFE trial), but may be used if massive transfusion needs (cheaper to use crystalloid + later add albumin if protein loss >20g/dL). Over-resuscitation increases ARDS risk → permissive hypotension concept (MAP 65 sufficient, avoid excessive fluids). De-escalation: slow diuretics once stabilized.

Minutes critical: immediate IM epinephrine (0.3-0.5 mg for adult, 0.3 mg for <30 kg). Position: supine, elevate legs. IV access, fluids, antihistamines (diphenhydramine), corticosteroids (methylprednisolone). Avoid lying supine initially if respiratory symptoms (fatal arrhythmia risk from epinephrine). Repeat epinephrine every 5-15 min if needed. Intubation may be needed (angioedema laryngeal airway). Hospital admission even if good response (biphasic reaction possible 4-72h later). Identify/avoid trigger. Consider epinephrine auto-injector prescription for at-risk.

Type I hypersensitivity: antigen cross-links IgE on mast cell/basophil surface → degranulation → release of: histamine (vasodilation, bronchospasm), tryptase (protease), leukotrienes (bronchoconstriction), prostaglandins, platelet-activating factor. Results: urticaria/pruritus, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension, shock, cardiac arrhythmias. Common triggers: medications (beta-lactam antibiotics, NSAIDs, ACE-I), foods (peanuts, shellfish, tree nuts), latex, hymenoptera (bee/wasp sting), contrast media. Diagnosis: elevated tryptase during event (correlates with degranulation degree).

Acute respiratory distress within 6h of transfusion. Presents with: hypoxemia, bilateral infiltrates, pulmonary edema, hypotension. Mortality 5-10%. Mechanism unclear but likely: immune (HLA/HNA antibodies in donor plasma activate recipient neutrophils → cytokine release), non-immune (storage-related factors). Risk: FFP, platelets, pRBCs all implicated. No specific treatment (supportive care, mechanical ventilation). Diagnosis of exclusion. Prevention: limit plasma transfusions, volume-controlled transfusion, consider male-only FFP donors (women have higher antibody prevalence).

SvO2 <60% indicates inadequate O2 delivery relative to demand. Measured via Swan-Ganz (PA catheter) or central line. ScvO2 (central venous) correlates with SvO2 (simpler, non-invasive). Low SvO2 + high lactate = tissue hypoxia (shock). High SvO2 (paradoxically >70%) + elevated lactate = maldistribution (septic shock, mitochondrial dysfunction). Treatment tailored: low SvO2 → increase CO (fluids, inotropes), increase oxygen delivery (blood transfusion, O2), low SvO2 + low lactate → volume needed. Trends over time more useful than single values.

metadata.topic: Mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO2) and lactate dynamics

text: Hyperglycemia common (stress response, decreased insulin sensitivity). Tight glycemic control (80-110 mg/dL) not superior to conventional (180-250 mg/dL) per NICE-SUGAR trial (increased mortality with tight control). Current goal: avoid severe hyperglycemia (>300 mg/dL, osmolar state). Insulin resistance pronounced in sepsis → large doses needed. Avoid hypoglycemia (seizures, arrhythmias, impaired immune function). Monitor frequently (q 1-2h in shock). Dextrose-containing fluids may worsen hyperglycemia—use judiciously. Re-evaluate target goals patient-specifically.

Sepsis triggers paradoxical response: initial hyper-inflammation (excess TNF, IL-6) followed by immunosuppression (T-cell exhaustion, reduced monocyte HLA-DR expression). Immunosuppressed phase associated with worse outcomes. Emerging therapies: GM-CSF (enhance monocyte function), IL-7 (T-cell recovery), checkpoint inhibitors (experimental). Current standard: supportive care only. Immunosuppressant avoidance (avoid prolonged corticosteroids >7 days if possible, controversial). Future: personalized immunotherapy based on immune profiling.

metadata.topic: Immune dysfunction in sepsis and immunotherapy

text: Weaning timing uncertain—generally attempt once MAP maintained at target (65 mmHg) without escalation for >6-12h. Gradual reduction: decrease infusion rate by 10-20% q 4-6h while monitoring BP, lactate, perfusion markers. Some patients require prolonged vasopressor support (>7 days)—associated with worse prognosis. Early vasopressor weaning associated with relapse of hypotension. Catch-22: long-term vasopressor use worsens outcomes but premature weaning causes relapse. Ongoing fluid optimization, infection source control, and inotropic support facilitate weaning.

VILI (ventilator-induced lung injury): volutrauma (overdistension of alveoli), barotrauma (high airway pressures), atelectotrauma (repeated opening/closing). Mechanisms: direct alveolar disruption, inflammatory cascade from cyclical reopening/collapse, increased microvascular permeability. Prevention: lung-protective ventilation (6-8 mL/kg ideal BW, Pplat <30). PEEP recruitment strategy: improves compliance, prevents atelectotrauma. Mortality benefit shown with lung-protective ventilation in ARDS (ARDSnet trial). Current standard for all mechanically ventilated patients.

metadata.topic: Volutrauma and barotrauma in mechanically ventilated patients

text: IBW = 50 + 2.3 * (height in inches - 60) for males, females = 45.5 + 2.3 * (height in inches - 60). Tidal volume 6-8 mL/kg IBW (lower end safer in ARDS). Example: 70 kg male 5'10'' (70 inches): IBW = 50 + 2.3 * 10 = 73 kg. 6-8 mL/kg × 73 = 438-584 mL appropriate TV. Helps prevent excessive ventilation (use actual weight might overdrive large patients). Frequent error: using current weight instead of IBW (leads to excessive TV, higher Pplat, worse outcomes).

metadata.topic: Ideal body weight calculation and tidal volume

text: Sustained inflation: stepwise increase in PEEP/pressure to high levels (30-40 cm H2O) for 30 sec. Goal: recruit collapsed alveoli → improve oxygenation + compliance. Open lung approach: high PEEP (15-20+) strategy throughout ventilation. Risk: hemodynamic compromise (reduced preload from high intrathoracic pressure), barotrauma if excessive. Efficacy variable: works in some ARDS patients (improves P/F ratio), neutral or worsening in others. Not universally recommended but may help refractory hypoxemia. Monitor BP, CO closely.

PaCO2 >50 mmHg tolerated to reduce TV/driving pressure. Respiratory acidosis develops (pH may drop to 7.15-7.20). Effects: sympathetic stimulation (tachycardia, hypertension), cerebral vasodilation (ICP concern in head trauma), catecholamine release (myocardial O2 demand increase), rightward O2-Hb curve shift (more O2 unloading to tissues). Renal buffering compensates (takes hours). Beneficial: reduced VILI. Contraindicated: intracranial hypertension, acute MI, pulmonary HTN (may worsen RV failure). Sodium bicarbonate if severe acidemia (rare need).

Sedation: morphine, fentanyl (analgesia + sedation), propofol (sedation only), dexmedetomidine (alpha-2 agonist, preserves cognition). Neuromuscular blockade: cisatracurium, vecuronium, rocuronium (paralytics). Indications for paralysis: profound dyssynchrony, high driving pressure despite sedation, mechanical ventilator limitations. ARDS: early paralysis (cisatracurium) improves outcomes (ACURASYS trial—reduced mortality, ICU-acquired weakness paradoxically lower despite paralysis). Daily sedation interruption improves outcomes (shorter vent time, reduced delirium). Reversibility of paralysis can be monitored (TOF ratio).

metadata.topic: Sedation and neuromuscular blockade in mechanically ventilated

text: Mismatch between patient effort and ventilator delivery: patient inhales while ventilator delivering exhalation (double-trigger), patient exhales during ventilator inspiration. Consequences: worsened oxygenation, increased work of breathing, patient distress, increased VILI risk. Causes: inadequate sedation, pain, hypoxemia, hypercarbia, ventilator settings (low trigger sensitivity, short expiration time). Management: adequate sedation/analgesia, adjust trigger sensitivity, increase inspiratory time (if triggering issue), decrease RR if excessive respiratory drive, neuromuscular blockade if severe.

Sinusitis from prolonged intubation (prevent with frequent suctioning, head of bed 30 degrees). Tracheal stenosis: thermal injury from ETT cuff, prolonged high cuff pressures (goal 25-30 cm H2O). Tracheomalacia: cuff-induced injury. Laryngeal edema/paralysis: nerve compression or direct injury. Tube obstruction: secretions, blood clot (suction, saline flushes, tube exchange if impacted). Tube migration: into right mainstem or extubated inadvertently. Accidental extubation: catastrophic if can't reintubate (bedside reintubation attempted). Prevention: appropriate cuff pressures, regular suctioning, secure fixation, sedation adequacy.

Indicated: anticipated >2 weeks mechanical ventilation, difficult airway management, neuromuscular disease (weakness), high aspiration risk. Timing: typically weeks 7-14 (earlier for some conditions). Benefits: reduced sedation, improved comfort, easier weaning, long-term access. Risks: procedure-related (hemorrhage, esophageal injury, misplacement), late complications (stenosis, tracheomalacia, trachea-innominate fistula). Tube changes: every 7-14 days to prevent obstruction, encrustation. Speaking valve allows phonation (requires adequate glottic closure, patient cooperation). Eventual decannulation goal if possible.

Reintubation within 48h = failed extubation (increases mortality, length of stay). Risk factors: age >65, ICU stay >7 days, cardiac disease, COPD, female sex, obesity, opioid use. Predictors: RSBI, CROP index (weak predictors individually). Prevention: structured weaning protocol, daily SBT once ready, avoid prolonged sedation, optimize strength (rehabilitation), cough assessment (adequate suctioning), address underlying cause (cardiac edema, sepsis), post-extubation non-invasive support (high-flow O2, CPAP, BiPAP) in high-risk patients.

Delivers heated/humidified blended gas at high flows (20-60 L/min). Provides PEEP ~3-5 cm H2O (flow-dependent), better humidification than standard nasal cannula, washout of anatomic dead space → reduced CO2. Improves comfort, oxygenation post-extubation. May reduce reintubation risk in high-risk patients (FLORALI trial: non-significant reduction but trend). Easier to implement than BiPAP (better tolerated). Increasingly used as first-line post-extubation support (especially COPD, obesity, post-operative). Failure rate 10-15%.

CMV/AC: guarantees minute ventilation, but impairs spontaneous breathing (deconditioning). Assist/control with low set rate allows spontaneous breaths. Synchronized IMV (SIMV): patient's spontaneous breaths pressure-supported, set rate as backup (reduces work but improves outcomes vs. CMV alone). Pressure support (PSV): patient initiates all breaths, weaning accomplished by decreasing PSV (5-15 cm H2O). No single mode superior—individual patient factors. Weaning mode less important than structured protocol (daily SBT, gradual support reduction). Some data suggesting early spontaneous breathing (CPAP early) improves outcomes.

metadata.topic: Ventilator mode selection and weaning strategy

text: PA pressure normally 20-30/10-15 mmHg, mean 15-20. Elevated SYSTOLIC (>40): pulmonary HTN, ARDS, mitral stenosis, hypervolemia. Elevated DIASTOLIC (>20): LV dysfunction (elevated PAWP), mitral stenosis, ARDS. PAWP (wedge pressure) reflects LA pressure: elevated (>18) suggests pulmonary edema risk. Regular PA pressure waveform: systolic rise from RV contraction, diastolic phase with a (RV contraction remnant), v (passive RA filling). Absence of a wave: atrial fibrillation.

metadata.topic: Pulmonary artery pressure monitoring and interpretation

text: CI (cardiac index) = CO / BSA (body surface area). Normal 2.5-4 L/min/m2. DO2 (oxygen delivery) = CI × CaO2 × 10, normal 500-600 mL/min/m2. VO2 (oxygen consumption) = (CaO2 - CvO2) × CO × 10, normal 200-250 mL/min/m2. DO2/VO2 ratio indicates supply-demand balance. Low DO2 with high VO2 (extraction) = compensated shock (tissue extracting maximally). Low DO2 with low VO2 = uncoupling (mitochondrial dysfunction, sepsis).

metadata.topic: Cardiac index and oxygen delivery calculations

text: Lusitropy = diastolic relaxation. Positive lusitrope = improved relaxation (better filling). Negative lusitrope = worsened relaxation. Milrinone: positive inotrope + positive lusitrope (improves both systolic function and relaxation—particularly useful in HF with diastolic dysfunction). Dobutamine: positive inotrope but increases myocardial stiffness (negative lusitropic effect). Calcium channel blockers: reduce contractility but improve lusitropy. In HF, improved lusitropy crucial—milrinone advantageous in this context.

Catecholamine surge (extreme stress, critical illness, high-dose vasopressors) → transient systolic dysfunction (apical ballooning typical, but midventricular/basal variants exist). Mimics MI (elevated troponin, ST changes), but coronaries normal on angiography. Usually reversible within days-weeks. Risk: hemodynamic instability, arrhythmias, shock. Management: supportive care, avoid excessive catecholamines if possible (use milrinone instead), mechanical support if cardiogenic shock. Prognosis generally good (recovery expected). Diagnosis requires high suspicion.

Bleeding most common ECMO complication (30-40% of patients). From: anticoagulation requirement, coagulopathy development, surgical sites, cannulation sites, GI bleeding, intracranial hemorrhage. Management: optimize anticoagulation (ACT 180-200), transfuse PRBCs/FFP/platelets, consider reversal agents (FFP, prothrombin complex concentrate if warfarin), vitamin K if deficient. Massive bleeding may require temporarily reducing heparin (thrombosis risk), transfusion target higher. Prophylactic measures: minimize blood draws, maintain FiO2 goal, avoid aggressive anticoagulation unless thrombosis develops.

metadata.topic: ECMO complications in detail: bleeding management

text: LVAD reduces LV workload → improved EF recovery potential, but RV must now handle increased blood volume from decompressed LV. RV dysfunction (from sepsis, ARDS, PE, infarction) → LVAD outflow obstruction risk. Presents: elevated CVP, low CO despite normal LVAD flows, pulmonary edema, decreased urine output. Prevention: optimize RV function pre-LVAD (inotropes, inhaled nitric oxide, mechanical support if severe). Management: inhaled nitric oxide, milrinone, inhaled epoprostenol, potentially RV support (RVAD/temporary ECMO). Right-sided LVAD failure is major reason for worse outcomes in some cohorts.

Measures myocardial deformation (shortening). Global longitudinal strain (GLS) normal -17% to -21% (negative = normal systolic shortening). Reduced GLS (e.g., -10%) indicates systolic dysfunction (may be present with normal EF—occult dysfunction). Circumferential strain assesses radial function. Strain detects early LV dysfunction before EF drops. Useful in: early recognition of cardiotoxicity (chemotherapy), prognostication (worse GLS = worse prognosis), viability assessment. Technical: requires good acoustic window, operator expertise. Increasingly available, becoming standard in major centers.

RV function complex (function depends on afterload unlike LV). Measures: TAPSE (tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion, normal >16 mm), RV S' (tissue Doppler, normal >10 cm/s), RV fractional area change (FAC, normal >35%), RV index of myocardial performance (RIMP, ratio of isovolumetric time to ejection time). Global RV dysfunction: dilation, septal flattening, reduced function on all measures. RV-LV interdependence: septal shift leftward → reduced LV filling (tamponade physiology). RV assessment increasingly recognized as important for prognosis/management decisions.

Atropine: removed from asystole/PEA algorithms (no benefit shown). Calcium chloride vs gluconate: both effective but gluconate preferred (less tissue damage if extravasated). Procainamide: no longer recommended (too slow, more side effects than amiodarone/lidocaine). Buffers: sodium bicarbonate only specific scenarios (not routine). Current emphasis: high-quality CPR > medications. Medications are 'fallback' to support CPR, not primary therapy.

metadata.topic: Medications NOT recommended in arrest anymore

text: Signs: no condensation in tube, no breath sounds bilateral, epigastric sounds, low ETCO2 (<10), waveform absent on capnography, tube position visualization difficult. Immediate action: pull tube, ventilate with bag-mask, reattempt intubation. Post-intubation: always confirm tube position (visualize cords, ETCO2, chest X-ray). Complication: severe hypoxemia if not recognized quickly (delays CPR). Prevention: proper sizing, depth marking at lips (typically 22-23 cm at teeth), direct visualization of cords when possible.

J wave = distinctive deflection at junction between QRS and ST segment, prominent in hypothermia. Osborn wave = exaggerated J wave (prominent hump). Indicates severe hypothermia (<32°C). PR/QRS/QT prolongation. Bradycardia (HR may be as low as 30 bpm). These findings dramatic but prognosis NOT hopeless—allow extracorporeal rewarming, prolonged resuscitation can result in full recovery. In severe hypothermia, patient should NOT be pronounced dead until core temperature rises to normal (and remains warm without ROSC).

metadata.topic: Hypothermia cardiac arrest: J waves and Osborn waves

text: IV (peripheral): rapid, accessible, preferred. IO (intraosseous): proximal humerus, proximal/distal tibia, effective, NO significant delay vs IV. ETT: absorption unpredictable, lower drug concentration reaching systemic circulation, requires removal for continued intubation. Intravenous access attempts: <30 sec per attempt recommended, move to IO if failed. Central line: not recommended during resuscitation (interrupts CPR, doesn't improve outcomes). Post-ROSC: central access can be established if peripheral inaccessible.

metadata.topic: Medication administration routes in arrest comparison

text: Multiple trials (ARREST, ALIVE) show amiodarone superior to lidocaine for shock-resistant VF (higher ROSC rates, ~20-30% higher). Mortality benefit unclear (similar hospital discharge rates). Lidocaine: faster onset, shorter elimination, fewer drug interactions. Amiodarone: loading 300 mg bolus, slower onset but longer duration. Both acceptable per guidelines; institution choice. Cost consideration (amiodarone expensive, lidocaine cheap). Combination rarely used (increased risk of torsades/QT prolongation).

metadata.topic: Amiodarone vs Lidocaine efficacy in VT/VF

text: Sodium bicarbonate 1 mEq/kg IV indicated: tricyclic antidepressant overdose (wide QRS/hypotension), severe hyperkalemia (peaked T waves, cardiac standstill risk), severe systemic acidosis (pH <7.1 from prolonged arrest). NOT routine (may worsen intracellular acidosis paradoxically, hypertonicity, hypokalemia). Use cautiously if at all—aggressive ventilation usually addresses respiratory component. Consider if bicarbonate-responsive condition identified. Monitor pH trending. May need repeated doses every 5-10 min.

metadata.topic: Bicarbonate in acidotic arrest: when indicated

text: If no ROSC in 4 minutes, consider delivering baby. Gravid uterus compresses IVC → reduces preload, critical for successful resuscitation. Delivery improves maternal hemodynamics immediately. Cesarean delivery ideally in OR (vertical incision recommended, avoid horizontal if time constraint), but if resuscitation failing and no immediate OR access—bedside delivery possible (lower segment vertical incision). Baby delivery urgent even if mother unstable. Both mother and baby may have better outcomes post-delivery than prolonged CPR alone.

OHCA = out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. Scoop and run: rapid transport to hospital (focus on CPR in transit, minimal on-scene time). Treat and load: initiate ACLS on scene (establish IV, medications, possibly intubation, extended time). Modern trend: balanced approach (initial stabilization then rapid transport). Data: time to defibrillation critical (<3-5 min VF prognosis excellent, >15 min poor). Advanced life support (IV, drugs) less critical than defibrillation/CPR time. Early mobilization to hospital preferred if defibrillation available en route.

metadata.topic: Scoop and run vs treat and load in OHCA

text: Risk: vomitus/secretions → aspiration pneumonia post-ROSC. Prevention: aggressive airway suctioning pre-intubation, head down position (if possible without compromising CPR), suction at ready for intubation attempt. Intubation cuff: verify position, confirm seal. Rapid sequence intubation (RSI) during resuscitation: cricoid pressure debatable (may impede view), sedation/paralysis for intubation needed. ETCO2 monitoring: ensures airway positioning. Post-ROSC: aspiration precautions (NPO, head of bed 30 degrees) and monitoring for ARDS.

Defibrillate VF/VT as soon as possible: each minute delay → ~10% reduction in survival. AED deployment: <10 min from collapse ideal for out-of-hospital. Hospital arrest: defibrillation within seconds usually possible. If prolonged asystole (>10 min) before defibrillation, single shock followed by continued CPR (rather than multiple shocks). Pacing for asystole: NOT recommended (no survival benefit shown). Asystole = worst prognosis regardless of intervention.

During cardiac arrest, severe acidosis develops (CO2 accumulation + anaerobic metabolism + lactate). Once thought protective (decreased metabolic rate), now recognized as harmful (impairs cellular function, catecholamine responsiveness). Treatment: hyperventilation post-intubation to reduce CO2 (but not excessive—avoid respiratory alkalosis which worsens hypocalcemia/hypokalemia). Bicarbonate: may worsen intracellular acidosis paradoxically. Best treatment = restore circulation (CPR, ECPR if available). Permissive hypercapnia concept applies post-arrest differently than mechanical ventilation.

metadata.topic: Metabolic acidosis in arrest: protective or harmful

text: Normal QTc varies by age: newborns <460 ms, infants/children <450 ms, adolescents/adults <440 ms males, <460 ms females. Pediatric drugs with QT risk: sotalol (used for SVT), ondansetron (nausea), domperidone. Congenital Long QT more common in children (LQTS 1-17). Risk of torsades higher with multiple risk factors (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, bradycardia, rapid infusions). Monitor closely in pediatric population. Electrolyte supplementation crucial (K+ >3.5, Mg >2).

Common: sinus bradycardia (vagal response), PVCs (hypoxemia, hypercarbia, inadequate anesthesia depth), atrial arrhythmias (airway stimulation, light anesthesia). Inhalation induction (especially halothane) → junctional rhythms, premature beats common (usually benign). Rapid-sequence intubation: etomidate/propofol apnea for few seconds acceptable, position airway quickly. Avoid halothane in patients at risk for arrhythmia (catecholamine sensitivity higher with halothane than isoflurane/sevoflurane). Epinephrine with halothane risk of arrhythmia (use <1.5-2 mcg/kg with halothane, higher doses with others). Ensure adequate IV access before induction (arrhythmia support preparation).

ABC approach: 1) Airway/Breathing/Circulation stability? 2) Rate control (target <110 bpm at rest initially, <130 with activity). 3) Identify reversible cause: hypoxemia, hypercarbia, infection, sepsis, hyperthyroidism, MI, PE. Troponin/ECG to exclude ACS. Thyroid function. Chest X-ray for pulmonary cause. Echocardiography to assess structure (structural disease = anticoagulation essential). Anticoagulation: initiate unless clear reason not to (anticoagulation within hours recommended to prevent thromboembolic events). Rate control more urgent than rhythm control in most cases.

metadata.topic: Atrial fibrillation new-onset: urgent workup priorities

text: Side effects: chest discomfort (15-20% patients, very frightening but benign), flushing, dyspnea, palpitations, light-headedness, transient asystole (normal finding). Contraindications: severe asthma/COPD (risk of severe bronchospasm), decompensated HF (may precipitate pulmonary edema transiently), recent use of dipyridamole/carbamazepine (increase adenosine effect). High-degree AV block (contraindication). Caution: elderly (may tolerate poorly), high-dose caffeine intake (antagonizes adenosine). Administration: rapid IV push with saline flush immediately after (absorption <10 sec). Central line allows smaller doses (less effective peripheral). Repeat doses: can escalate (6 mg → 12 mg).

Catecholamines (dopamine, epinephrine, dobutamine): receptor downregulation + phosphodiesterase upregulation. Amiodarone: less tachyphylaxis (multi-channel effects). Sotalol: decreasing effectiveness with continuous use. Solutions: rotate agents (different mechanisms), intermittent dosing, increase dose (if tolerated), combination therapy. Clinical pearl: amiodarone useful for refractory VF (less tachyphylaxis than other agents). Dopamine >6 hours often requires escalation. Milrinone may develop tolerance (tachyphylaxis) after 24-48h—consider adding or switching agent.

Therapeutic digoxin: 0.8-2 ng/mL. Levels >2 ng/mL risk of toxicity (narrow margin). Measurement: typically done 6+ hours post-dose, 5+ days after initiating/changing dose (steady state). Hypokalemia increases toxicity risk (even at therapeutic levels). Hypomagnesemia also increases risk. Acute loading: 10-15 mcg/kg (usually as divided doses q 6h to assess tolerance). Maintenance: 5-10 mcg/kg/day divided. Renal failure: requires dose reduction (clearance kidney-dependent). Drug interactions: quinidine, verapamil, amiodarone all increase digoxin levels. Antidigoxin Fab (DigiBind, DigiTab) for life-threatening toxicity.

Procainamide class IA antiarrhythmic. Long-term use (>1 year) associated with drug-induced lupus (antihistone antibodies develop in ~50% chronic users, clinical lupus in 1-3%). Presents: arthralgias, fever, pericarditis (can progress to pericardial tamponade). Diagnosed: positive ANA + anti-histone antibodies, ESR elevation. Management: discontinue procainamide, symptoms usually resolve within weeks. NSAIDs for symptom management. Corticosteroids if severe/refractory. Rechallenge risks recurrence. Alternative antiarrhythmics preferred for long-term use (amiodarone, flecainide, sotalol).

Severe prolonged cough → increased intrathoracic pressure → reduced venous return → syncope (usually benign). Risk: mechanical injury, rib fractures, hemoptysis. Some patients develop arrhythmias (usually benign, self-terminating). Mechanism: sudden pressure changes + hypoxemia (cough reduces ventilation) + sympathetic activation. Risk factors: smoking, COPD, pertussis. Prevention: bronchodilators, cough suppressants, smoking cessation. Syncope typically lasts <1 min, patient falls/strikes head (injury risk). Differentiate from cardiac arrhythmia syncope (cardiac usually sudden without preceding cough). Workup: ECG, Holter if recurrent episodes.

Exaggerated response to carotid sinus stimulation (massage, neck turning). Presents: syncope with head turning, shaving. Mechanism: parasympathetic activation → bradycardia (cardioinhibitory type) or vasodilation (vasodepressor type) or mixed. More common: elderly (>70), males. Diagnosis: carotid massage (with ECG monitoring, in supine initially then upright) showing >3 sec asystole or >50 mmHg SBP drop = positive (reproducible response = diagnostic). Management: pacemaker if cardioinhibitory type (bradycardia relief). Avoid tight collars, neck turning triggers. Usually reassurance + fall prevention sufficient if vasodepressor type.

Red flags: exertional syncope (during/immediately post-exercise), sudden onset, no prodrome, family history of SCD, abnormal ECG. Workup: ECG mandatory (look for Long QT, Brugada, HCM features like LVH), stress test if exertional component. Echo if ECG abnormal or high suspicion. Holter monitor if palpitations. Genetic testing if family history suggestive (CPVT, ARVC, Long QT). Management: restrict activity until diagnosis made and cleared (some athletes may have ICD placed). Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy #1 cause SCD in athletes—echo crucial. Commotio cordis (blunt chest impact) less common but important in young athletes.

metadata.topic: Syncope in young athlete: concerning features

text: Type A = hypoxic tissue hypoperfusion (classic shock). Type B = non-hypoxic causes (medications, toxins, liver disease, B1=underlying disease without hypoperfusion, B2=drugs/toxins, B3=liver failure). Clear distinction: A requires intervention for perfusion, B requires treating etiology. B3 (liver failure) particularly resistant to treatment—mortality high. Some data: lactate normalization slower in liver failure. Glucose control crucial in type B (impaired gluconeogenesis). Lactate kinetics different (B lactate may NOT clear despite improved perfusion—depends on liver function).

metadata.topic: Lactic acidosis type A vs B clarification

text: Myocardial dysfunction from: TNF-alpha direct cardiotoxicity, systemic inflammatory mediators, coronary vasospasm, microvascular thrombosis, mitochondrial dysfunction. Presents: dilated LV, reduced EF, elevated troponin (mild), pulmonary edema. Usually resolves within 7-10 days if sepsis controlled. Prognosis: associated with worse outcomes (mortality ~50% vs ~20% in sepsis without cardiomyopathy). Management: aggressive source control, antibiotics, fluids (careful—avoid overload), inotropes (dobutamine, milrinone), vasopressors. Beta-blockers controversial (may worsen acutely, but long-term may benefit). Mechanical support if refractory shock.

Relative adrenal insufficiency: inadequate cortisol response to stress (ACTH stimulation test abnormal—delta cortisol <9 mcg/dL with 250 mcg ACTH bolus). Risk: prolonged critical illness, sepsis, prior corticosteroid use, pituitary surgery. Diagnosis controversial (testing not standardized). Treatment controversial: low-dose hydrocortisone (50 mg q6h) in refractory septic shock may help (CORTICUS trial, improved shock reversal but no mortality benefit). Not routine. Assess baseline cortisol + ACTH (random level high-normal may indicate inadequacy in acute setting). Empiric corticosteroid coverage reasonable in refractory shock.

Chylothorax = lymphatic fluid in pleural space (milky appearance). Causes: thoracic surgery (especially esophageal), malignancy, trauma, spontaneous (rare). Large chylothorax can cause significant fluid loss → hypoproteinemia, lipid loss, immune dysfunction, hemodynamic collapse if untreated. Diagnosis: pleural fluid triglycerides >200 mg/dL (or >higher than serum), cholesterol <200, chylomicrons present. Management: NPO (reduces chylus production), chest tube drainage, medium-chain triglyceride diet (absorbed via portal blood vs lacteal system). Surgery if persistent despite conservative care. Nutritional support: TPN with lipids restricted (alternatively, fat-restricted diet).

Liver failure = loss of synthetic function (albumin, clotting factors), metabolic dysfunction (hypoglycemia, hyperammonemia), vasodilation (portal HTN, splanchnic vasodilation). In shock: further compromised (hepatic ischemia from low flow). Lactate clearance impaired (liver primary organ for clearance)—lactate elevation very ominous. Coagulopathy severe (low platelets, low factors, DIC often concurrent). Encephalopathy (hyperammonemia, false neurotransmitters). Management: supportive, glucose management (hypoglycemia risk), mannitol or lactulose for ammonia, FFP for coagulopathy (temporary), N-acetylcysteine being studied. Prognosis: poor (MELD score predicts outcomes). Transplant evaluation if potential candidate.

Differential: inadequate perfusion (hypovolemia despite fluid—reassess IV access), obstruction (tamponade, PE, dissection), pump failure (cardiogenic, myocarditis), overwhelming sepsis (refractory distributive shock), adrenal insufficiency, anaphylaxis (late phase with refractoriness). Workup: physical exam (JVP, lung sounds, heart sounds), imaging (echo, CXR), labs (lactate, troponin, cortisol, complement levels if anaphylaxis suspected). Escalation: add second vasopressor (epinephrine if on NE), inotrope addition (dobutamine, milrinone), mechanical support (IABP, ECMO, ECPR). Acidosis correction may improve responsiveness (sodium bicarbonate if severe). Source control absolute priority (especially sepsis).

metadata.topic: Refractory hypotension despite vasopressors and fluids

text: Current evidence: crystalloids preferred over colloids (albumin, hetastarch, dextran) for initial resuscitation. SAFE trial: albumin no better than crystalloid in general sepsis (same mortality). Albumin may increase mortality in traumatic brain injury (avoid). Hetastarch increased mortality in sepsis (avoid). Gelatin/dextran: limited modern data. Cost: crystalloids much cheaper. Strategy: initial crystalloid resuscitation (30 mL/kg LR in sepsis), transition to albumin only if massive transfusion requirements (proteinuria from extravasation, decreased oncotic pressure, ongoing losses >20g/day protein). Balanced crystalloids (LR, Plasmalyte) preferred over normal saline (hyperchloremic acidosis risk).

Concept: maintain lower BP (MAP 50-65 mmHg acceptable) to reduce ongoing bleeding and coagulopathy worsening (high-pressure bleeding increases hemorrhage). Standard: allow BP to be 'permissive' until bleeding controlled (surgical). Not for head trauma (risk of secondary brain injury). Transfusion: damage control approach—1:1:1 ratio PRBC:FFP:platelets (not sequential transfusion). Early surgical control paramount. Damage control resuscitation principles: minimize crystalloids, maximize blood product use, use vasopressors sparingly (prioritize hemorrhage control). Prognosis: hemorrhage control critical—BP manipulation alone insufficient if ongoing bleeding.

Inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) activated by inflammatory mediators in sepsis. NO production excessive → vasodilation, hypotension, cardiomyopathy, multi-organ dysfunction. Septic shock = partly NO-mediated. Potential therapy: NOS inhibition (has been studied but increased mortality in trials—NOS essential for immune function). Instead: restore vasomotor tone (vasopressors), improve tissue perfusion, control inflammation (source control, antibiotics). L-arginine (NO substrate) not helpful. Selective pulmonary vasodilation (inhaled NO, sildenafil) useful for RV dysfunction/pulmonary HTN. Understanding NO important for conceptualizing septic shock pathophysiology.

Splanchnic vasoconstriction in shock (sympathetic response, catecholamine effect) → bowel ischemia risk. Presents: severe abdominal pain, bowel dysfunction, metabolic acidosis (lactate from ischemic bowel), blood-stained stool, peritonitis if perforation. Diagnosis: CT with IV contrast (bowel wall enhancement abnormality, portal air), endoscopy if suspicion high. Management: resuscitation (improve perfusion), discontinue vasoconstrictors if possible (switch to milrinone), vasodilators (nitrates, nitroglycerin) being studied. Surgical resection if perforation/transmural necrosis confirmed. Prevention: adequate resuscitation, avoid excessive vasopressors (necessary evil balance). Monitor for abdominal complications during critical illness.

Pediatric: weaning principles similar but age-specific: spontaneous breathing trials shorter (5-10 min initially), smaller TV/weight-based dosing. Obesity: delayed weaning (sedative metabolism impaired), may need higher PEEP, prone positioning helpful if needed. Neuromuscular disease: ICU-acquired weakness common—aggressive rehabilitation, avoid paralytic agents if possible, extended weaning. Cardiac disease: careful fluid management during weaning (pulmonary edema risk). COPD: aggressive diuresis NOT indicated (may precipitate respiratory failure), gentle weaning, avoid rapid pressure reduction.

Rare but important complication: excessive negative pressure during inspiration → fluid transudation into alveoli. Causes: upper airway obstruction (laryngospasm, post-extubation stridor), heavy inspiratory effort against resistance, mechanical ventilation (high pressure settings). Presents: pink frothy sputum, hypoxemia post-extubation, rales. Usually self-limited if airway obstruction relieved. Management: oxygen, PEEP (if severe), diuretics controversial (some say avoid if true negative pressure pulmonary edema). Prevention: careful extubation (sufficient reversal of muscle relaxants, adequate spontaneous ventilation), humidified air post-extubation, treat laryngospasm immediately (positive pressure to overcome obstruction).

Different spectrum: fungal organisms (PCP, aspergillosis), viral (CMV, COVID-19, RSV), atypical bacteria (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia). Diagnosis same (bilateral infiltrates, hypoxemia, low PAWP). Management: lung-protective ventilation identical, antibiotics different (broad coverage including fungal/atypical until identified), immunologic support (IVIG, G-CSF potentially). Prognosis: worse than immunocompetent (mortality 40-80% depending on immune status). Prophylaxis critical (PCP prophylaxis in CD4 <200, antifungal prophylaxis in neutropenia). Consider early bronchoscopy with BAL to identify organism (guides therapy).

Strategies: oral care (chlorhexidine), semi-recumbent positioning (prevent microaspiration), spontaneous breathing trials (reduce ventilator days), subglottic secretion drainage (reduces VAP rates), avoid unnecessary sedation (early mobilization), prevent sinusitis (suctioning, maintain tube position). VAP definition controversial (clinical criteria vs microbiology-based). Incidence: ~1-3% per ventilator day in most ICUs. Mortality: increases length of stay 7-10 days, cost. Diagnosis: clinical (fever, leukocytosis, new infiltrate) + culture (endotracheal aspirate or BAL). Treatment: empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics de-escalated per culture.

Risk factors: emergency surgery (full stomach), obesity, GERD, pregnancy, recent meal, bowel obstruction, gastroparesis. Prevention: preoperative fasting (2h clear liquids, 6h solids recommended), pharmacologic (H2-blockers, antacids, prokinetics), RSI (rapid sequence intubation) with cricoid pressure (controversial—may impede view). Cricoid pressure technique: 10 N awake, 30 N after loss of consciousness. Induction: etomidate/propofol (avoid thiopental—no speed advantage, more respiratory depression), suxamethonium (rapid onset) OR rocuronium (slightly slower but no succinylation pseudoapnea issues). Post-extubation: NPO until fully alert, head of bed elevated.

Normal cuff pressure: 25-30 cm H2O (safe range). Excessive pressure (>30 cm H2O) → tracheal stenosis, mucosal ulceration, necrosis. Insufficient pressure (<20 cm H2O) → aspiration risk, decreased ventilation seal. Measurement: pressure gauge used q 8h or daily. Technique: minimal leak technique (inflate until no leak during positive pressure, then withdraw 0.5-1 mL air)—simple bedside method. Over-inflation common (staff inflates aggressively, thinking equals better seal). Risk: increases with: prolonged intubation, high ventilating pressures, large tube diameter. Monitoring: cuff pressure maintained, leak test routinely.

Failed intubation = catastrophic situation. Immediate: resume 100% O2 pre-oxygenation (bag-mask if possible), allow patient to wake up (stop induction agent, reverse neuromuscular blockade if given), prepare for alternative (awake fiberoptic, video laryngoscope, emergency tracheostomy). Avoid 'can't intubate, can't oxygenate' crisis: maintain spontaneous ventilation if possible during attempts (avoid paralysis until airway secured). Front-load: 100% O2 for 3-5 min pre-intubation (preoxygenation critical). Induction: use agents preserving airway tone (etomidate preferred, avoid propofol if hemodynamically unstable, succinylcholine for rapid onset). Video laryngoscopy improves success rates.

I:E ratio >1:1 (e.g., 2:1, 3:1). Prolonged inspiration maintains elevated mean airway pressure → recruitment. Discomfort common (patient sensation of breathing reversed—uncomfortable), dyssynchrony (patient fighting ventilator). Requires: sedation, often paralysis. Barotrauma/volutrauma risk (higher Pplat to achieve same recruitment compared to conventional). Modern opinion: conventional ventilation with optimized PEEP preferable (achieves recruitment without discomfort, reverse I:E rarely needed). Rescue therapy only for refractory hypoxemia despite high PEEP. If used: monitor Pplat closely, sedate heavily, plan for pressure weaning.

text: ARDS phase 1-2 (exudative): fluid conservative approach superior (ALVEOLI trial—lower target PAWP improved lung function). Fluid restriction strategy: target PAWP <18 mmHg, CVP <4 mmHg (permissive hypotension acceptable if MAP adequate). Diuretics: loop diuretics if positive fluid balance (even just monitoring without targets, negative balance associated with faster oxygenation improvement). Paradox: hypovolemia worsens organ perfusion but hypervolemia worsens ARDS. Balance critical: maintain organ perfusion while avoiding pulmonary edema. Phase 2 (fibrotic phase): less clear, may need some fluids (chronic phase different pathophysiology).

metadata.topic: Drying out vs fluid management in ARDS

text: Atmospheric pressure decreases at altitude → inspired O2 partial pressure decreases. FiO2 × atmospheric pressure = PiO2. At sea level: 0.21 × 760 = 160 mmHg inspired O2. At 10,000 ft: 0.21 × 500 = 105 mmHg inspired O2 (hypoxemia risk even with normal lungs). For mechanically ventilated: must increase FiO2 to maintain same PiO2. Implications: post-operative patient at altitude at higher hypoxemia risk, monitor SpO2 carefully, liberal O2 supplementation. Acclimatization (days to weeks): increased RBC production, hyperventilation help offset. Pulmonary edema risk (high altitude pulmonary edema/HAPE possible).

metadata.topic: Barometric pressure and high altitude effects

text: Infection: sepsis from contaminated catheter (incidence ~3-7 per 1000 catheter-days), requires removal, antibiotics. Thrombosis: catheter thrombus, pulmonary infarction risk (heparin coating decreases incidence). Arrhythmias: ventricular ectopy common during insertion (hitting RV wall), rarely VT/VF. Myocardial rupture: rare, catastrophic. Endocarditis: if bacteremia. Prevention: aseptic technique, regular heparin flushing, prompt removal when no longer needed (ideal <7 days). Monitoring: check position (chest X-ray), waveforms (assess for dampening, withdrawal), change dressing q 2-3 days. Risk-benefit: useful in cardiogenic shock, refractory hypotension; less clear benefit in sepsis (no mortality benefit shown).

Non-invasive transcutaneous pacing via esophageal electrodes. Advantages: less discomfort than transcutaneous thoracic pacing (esophageal positioned near atrium = lower threshold for capture), useful for severe bradycardia/blocks awaiting transvenous pacing. Disadvantages: esophageal placement required (cooperation needed), transient discomfort, not for emergency (slower than TCP). Rarely used in modern practice (transcutaneous pacing simpler, more accepted). Role: ICU setting in anticipating need for pacing (prophylactic placement) or bridge to transvenous in monitored setting. Technical: bipolar catheter in esophagus, output increased gradually until capture achieved.

Optimal timing: inflation at dicrotic notch (beginning of diastole), deflation just before systole. Improves diastolic pressure (increases coronary perfusion), reduces aortic impedance during systole (afterload reduction). Dysrhythmia effects: 1:2 counterpulsation (every other beat augmented) acceptable, 1:3 if AFib (variable RR can make 1:1 impossible). Low heart rates (<60): IABP support less effective (insufficient number of cycles). Tachycardia (>110): diastole shortened, IABP timing difficult. Doppler assessment: aortic flow analysis confirms diastolic augmentation. Improves hemodynamics transiently but mortality benefit unproven. Weaning: gradual reduction of frequency (1:2, then 1:4, then removal).

Beck triad: elevated JVP, muffled heart sounds, hypotension (classic but not always present). Kussmaul sign: paradoxical JVP rise on inspiration (ventricular interdependence, constrictive physiology). Pulsus paradoxus: >10 mmHg SBP drop with inspiration (mechanistic: inspiration increases RV preload, RV expands → septal bulge compresses LV). Physiology: pericardial fluid restricts filling at end-diastole (limits ventricular volume expansion). Echo: RA/RV diastolic collapse, swinging heart, respiratory variation >30% in inflow. Treatment: pericardiocentesis (emergent if hemodynamic instability). Post-procedure: repeat imaging, address etiology (infection, malignancy, post-cardiac surgery).

metadata.topic: Tamponade diagnosis: Beck vs Kussmaul vs pulsus

text: HFpEF = heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (EF >50% or ≥50%). Standard EF assessment misses HFpEF (EF normal!). Strain imaging detects early dysfunction: global longitudinal strain reduced (e.g., -10% instead of normal -17%), tissue Doppler e' reduced. Diastolic assessment: E/e' ratio >14 suggests elevated filling pressures. LV hypertrophy common (concentric), diastolic dysfunction prominent. Prognosis: better than HFrEF but still significant mortality/morbidity. Treatment: diuretics for symptoms, ACE-I/ARB for HTN/proteinuria, SGLT2 inhibitors emerging. Imaging critical for diagnosis (strain picks up dysfunction missed by EF alone).

IVC diameter + respiratory variation estimates CVP. Normal IVC: <2 cm, collapses >50% with inspiration (CVP 0-5 mmHg). Mildly elevated: 2-3 cm, collapses 25-50% (CVP 5-10 mmHg). Elevated: >3 cm, <25% collapse (CVP 10-20 mmHg). Markedly elevated: >3 cm, no collapse (CVP >20 mmHg). Limitations: body habitus (difficult to visualize obesity), mechanical ventilation (changes respiratory dynamics), ascites. Practical: useful bedside assessment when PAC unavailable, trends important (not absolute values). Correlation with clinical exam (JVP) helpful for validation.

text: Both: equal diastolic pressures, square root sign (dip-plateau), elevated PAWP. Differences: pericarditis has septal bounce on echo (RV-LV interaction), respiratory variation >25% in inflow, LV not thick. Cardiomyopathy: thick ventricular wall, less respiratory variation, myocardial infiltration may be visible. Imaging: CT/MRI can visualize thickened pericardium (constrictive). Catheter data: concordance of RV-LV systolic pressures more common in restrictive (discordance in constriction). Therapy: pericardiectomy for constriction, no surgical therapy for cardiomyopathy. Clinical context: post-cardiac surgery suggests constriction, infiltrative disease suggests cardiomyopathy (amyloidosis, sarcoidosis).

metadata.topic: Constrictive pericarditis vs restrictive cardiomyopathy differentiation

text: Demand ischemia: elevated MVO2 without increased supply (tachycardia, hypertension, sepsis). Type 2 MI per 4th Universal Definition. Presents: troponin elevation, ECG changes (may be diffuse, non-territorial). Treatment: address demand (beta-blockers, rate control), optimize perfusion (support BP, fluids if hypovolemic). Not typical ACS—coronaries likely normal. Prognosis: depends on underlying condition (sepsis prognosis worse). Mortality: elevated troponin = worse outcomes regardless of mechanism. Secondary prevention: optimize HTN/rate control. Differentiate from ACS: clinical context, coronary calcification on CT (supply limitation in ACS), troponin pattern (more gradual rise/fall in demand ischemia).

Dobutamine: escalated infusion (5-40 mcg/kg/min) can precipitate arrhythmias, MI, hemodynamic instability. Exercise: exertional syncope/chest pain contraindication (stop immediately). Mortality: <0.01% in non-high-risk patients, higher in unstable CAD. Contraindications: uncontrolled HTN (>180 SBP), severe aortic stenosis (LV outflow limitation), decompensated HF, unstable angina (unless already on catheterization), hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with outflow obstruction (exertional syncope risk). Safety: echo machine and resuscitation equipment available, real-time monitoring, IV access for adenosine reversal (if dobutamine used, can induce severe hypertension/arrhythmia). Stopping criteria: ischemia (wall motion abnormality), arrhythmia, hemodynamic instability, target HR achieved, exhaustion.

Mechanical valve: bright echo, restrictive motion (leaflets follow path), increased gradients normal. Bioprosthetic: thinner appearance, wider opening. Assessment: gradient (peak and mean), effective orifice area (EOA), regurgitation grade. Pannus: tissue overgrowth on valve (mechanical valves especially), can increase gradients, reduce EOA. Thrombosis: acute valve obstruction (mechanical valve emergency). Endocarditis: vegetation on valve, valve dehiscence, paravalvular regurgitation (complications). Structural deterioration: bioprosthetic leaflet calcification/restriction (years), mechanical valve rare (designed for durability). Doppler crucial (gradient change significant). Serial monitoring: baseline study comparison important for recognizing deterioration.
